items.md: Babbar, Kantor, Whalley, & Zeng (2026) ask whether mission-oriented public R&D pushes technological change toward automation, and whether this reaches local manufacturing labor markets. The setting is NASA's Space Race after Sputnik. The paper makes two contributions. First, it combines a full-text patent measure of automation versus augmentation (built following Autor, Chin, Salomons, and Seegmiller 2024) with a government-interest patent register. It shows that NASA-related patents are more automation-intensive than other patents, including within technology classes (Table 2). Second, it reuses the pre-Sputnik "space capability" exposure design of Kantor and Whalley (2025) to test whether exposed county-industry cells saw lower labor shares and a shifting skill mix from 1947 to 1992 (Tables 3-6). The authors read the labor-share results as evidence that public R&D shaped the direction of technology (pp. 3-5).

items.md: **Data.** Full-text US patents, 1930-2025, 10,636,023 observations (p. 10). NASA flags come from a government-interest patent register. Census of Manufactures county by two-digit SIC data for 1947, 1954, 1958, 1963, 1967, 1972, 1977, 1982, 1987 and 1992 supply labor share (wage bill over value added) and skill intensity (non-production over production workers) (pp. 11, 15). Space exposure comes from digitized CIA estimates of Soviet space capabilities, 1947-1991 (p. 12).

q.exact: Our labor share measure is defined as the ratio of the total wage bill to the value added of all manufacturing firms within a cell. Skill intensity is measured as the ratio of non-production to production workers in the same cell.

items.md: **Design.** Patent level: a linear probability model of an automation-intensive indicator (automation score above augmentation score) on a NASA indicator, with year and, in the last column, USPC technology fixed effects (equation 1, p. 14). Panel level: a triple difference across high versus low pre-1958 space capability, space versus non-space industries (transportation and electronics), and pre/Space Race/post periods (equation 2, p. 16):

q.exact: To assess whether labor market outcomes changed disproportionately in these county–industry cells, we estimate a triple-di↵erence specification that compares outcomes across high- and low-space capability pairs, before and after the Space Race, and between space-related and non-space industries.

items.md: The patent regressions use 2,742,807 observations (Table 2), drawn from the 10,636,023 patents in the full dataset; how the subset is selected is not reported in this version. The panel sample is restricted to counties with at least one patent in 1945-1958 and inside an MSA, cells observed in the 1958 Census and in at least eight census years, non-missing employment and value added, at least one space-related industry in the county, and excludes North Dakota, South Dakota and Wyoming (p. 13). The text reports 6,759 county-industry observations covering 86 counties and 19 two-digit SIC industries (p. 14), while Tables 3-5 report 6,717 observations. Table 1 reports 735 county-industry cells in 1958, 76 of them in space industries. Mean 1958 labor share is 0.26 (SD 0.26). The Space Race window is 1958-1972 and the post period 1973-1992 (p. 17); in the tables the Space Race years are 1963, 1967 and 1972 and the post years are 1977-1992. NASA accounted for 1% of GDP in 1966 (p. 4), and only 15% of federal R&D in 1966 was basic research (p. 3). The sample is large urban counties with prior patenting.

items.md: **Table B.1 — Validation Exercise 1: Correlation between Automation, Augmentation Scores and Firm-Level Employment.** With firm fixed effects the automation coefficient is -0.004 (SE 0.022) in column 5 and -0.041 (SE 0.019) in column 6 (p. 31).

**Causal plausibility.** The exposure logic is thoughtful: capability is predetermined and keyed to Soviet, not US, technology choices, and the shock is a foreign launch. Pre-trends are flat in 1947 and 1954 only, two pre-periods, and the figure's coefficients cannot be checked here. The design identifies a differential change for exposed space-industry cells; it does not identify automation.

**Automation is inferred, not measured.** The patent measure (Table 2) never enters the panel regressions (Tables 3-6). The link from "NASA patents automate" to "labor share fell in exposed cells" is an interpretation. Labor share is wage bill over value added, so a demand-driven rise in value added, rents, or capital-intensive expansion lowers it with no labor-saving technology at all. The paper does not separate these channels.

**Internal tensions in the text.** (1) Observations are 6,759 in the text but 6,717 in Tables 3-5. (2) The text says Table 5 local effects resemble Table 3, but the local triple terms fall from -0.28 to -0.04 (SE 0.08). (3) The market-exposure terms for non-space industries are significant (-0.25 with SE 0.08; -0.41 with SE 0.13, Table 5, col. 1), unaddressed in the text. (4) Skill coefficients of 0.13 (SE 0.06) and 0.50 (SE 0.10, Table 4 Panel B) are not zero. (5) p. 14 says automation varies little with safety orientation, but Table 2 shows 0.107. (6) The main text says IC patents have lower augmentation scores (p. 11), but Table B.2 shows a positive 0.018 (SE 0.004). (7) National labor-share estimates have an SE of 0.33 on a coefficient of -0.55.
**Validation is thin.** In Table B.1 the automation-employment correlation turns positive or near zero once other terms are removed (0.096, SE 0.040, col. 2; -0.004, col. 5).

**Transfer to 2-year college openings.** The design does not transfer directly: it needs a predetermined capability index crossed with a national shock, and openings have no such shock. Its text-similarity machinery could transfer, for instance matching local industry patent text to program offerings, and the county-by-2-digit-industry panel with MSA-by-year effects is a usable template for firm and industry-mix outcomes. The automation/augmentation score is a ready innovation-direction outcome. The sample, large urban MSAs with prior patents and data ending in 1992, is far from rural community college settings.
Test whether public R&D beyond NASA is also automation-intensive (p. 22).
Use individual-level data with education and career trajectories to detect distributional effects (p. 22).
Link the patent automation measure directly to the panel outcomes to test the mechanism.
Study how policy shapes the direction, not only the rate, of technological change as AI advances (p. 22).
Not reported in this version: sample selection for Table 2, clustering for patent regressions, and coefficients behind Figure 3.

The paper's headline is that public R&D can steer technology toward labor substitution, with persistent local labor-share effects and little visible change in skill composition. For researchers studying local R&D shocks, it is a reminder to measure the direction of innovation, not just its volume, and to report the share-of-value-added denominator problem. For the reader's project on college openings, the transferable pieces are the text-based patent measures of what kind of innovation follows an institutional change and the triple-difference logic that uses predetermined local capability. Future work should tie the patent-level direction measure to the local outcomes it is meant to explain, and show pre-trends with more than two pre-periods before treating labor-share declines as evidence of automation.
